title: Rajasthan Challenges Gujarat's GI Tag on Cumin and Fennel
excerpt: Farmers and scientists in Rajasthan are demanding revocation of Geographical Indication tags awarded to Unjha cumin and fennel, arguing Gujarat's largest spice market is a trading hub, not a production region.
body:
• Rajasthan's South Asia Biotechnology Centre has filed a formal objection with the GI Registry, seeking revocation of GI tags granted to Unjha cumin and fennel in Gujarat.
  • Scientists argue Unjha is primarily a spice trading hub, not a production region, and that claims of superior aroma and quality lack peer-reviewed scientific evidence.
  • Rajasthan farmers fear their produce — long sold through the Unjha market — will be rebranded under Gujarat's identity, eroding their ability to command premium prices.
  • GI-tagged products can command 20–30 per cent higher prices, making the certification a high-stakes fight for lakhs of farmers across both states.

A simmering dispute between India's two largest cumin-producing states has erupted into a full-blown intellectual property battle. Weeks after the Geographical Indications Registry in Chennai granted GI tags to "Unjha Cumin" and "Unjha Fennel" from Gujarat's Mehsana district, scientists and farmers in Rajasthan are pushing to have the certifications revoked.

The Objection

The Jodhpur-based South Asia Biotechnology Centre (SABC) has submitted a detailed report to the GI Registrar challenging both tags on scientific and legal grounds. The report raises eleven specific points — five against the cumin tag and six against the fennel tag — questioning whether the registrations meet the fundamental requirements of geographical indication law.

"The claims made regarding these two products are completely false. Both of these were registered on the same day, and they received the GI tag on the same day."

— Dr. Bhagirath Choudhary, Founder Director, South Asia Biotechnology Centre

At the heart of the objection is a deceptively simple question: does Unjha's reputation as a spice market equal geographic origin? SABC argues it does not. While Unjha is home to one of Asia's largest spice markets and serves as India's principal trading hub for cumin and fennel, much of the produce sold there is grown by farmers in western Rajasthan — in districts like Barmer, Jaisalmer, and Jodhpur for cumin, and Sirohi for fennel.

Missing Science

The SABC report takes particular aim at the scientific claims underpinning the GI applications. It states that no comparative laboratory reports, representative sampling, or peer-reviewed studies were presented to substantiate claims that Unjha cumin and fennel possess superior aroma, taste, or volatile oil content. The report notes that DUS (Distinctiveness, Uniformity and Stability) characteristics cited in the applications are meant for plant variety identification — not for proving the geographical distinctiveness required for a GI tag.

On fennel, the objection is even more pointed: premium fennel grown in the Abu Road area of Rajasthan's Sirohi district is routinely supplied to Gujarat's Unjha market. SABC contends this means the product's quality is tied to Rajasthan's geography and growing conditions, not Gujarat's.

What's at Stake

The financial implications are significant. According to government estimates, GI-tagged products can command prices 20 to 30 per cent higher than comparable untagged goods. For lakhs of cumin and fennel farmers across Rajasthan — many of whom have sold their harvest through the Unjha APMC for decades — losing the identity of their produce to a trading hub could mean lower prices and weakened bargaining power.

The dispute also has implications for future branding efforts. Rajasthan's farmers and scientists argue that if the Unjha tags remain, it could complicate any future attempt to secure separate GI recognition for Rajasthan-grown cumin and fennel, effectively locking the state's farmers out of the premium certification system.

Gujarat's Position

Gujarat's state government, which supported the GI applications through its Department of Horticulture and Farmers' Welfare, has framed the tags as a milestone for the spice sector. Dinesh Patel, Chairman of the Unjha APMC, has called the certification "historic," saying it will strengthen market credibility, boost exports, and create new opportunities for farmers. Gujarat is India's largest cumin producer and accounts for a significant share of the country's cumin exports globally.

What Happens Next

The objection now sits with the GI Registry in Chennai. SABC has formally requested a re-examination of the scientific evidence and legal processes behind both registrations. The centre has also asked that western Rajasthan's cumin and fennel be considered for their own geographical indication — a move that would establish the producing region's identity independently from the trading market.

Dr. Choudhary has stressed that the fight is not against Gujarat per se. "We are not against any state," he said. "Our objective is only about the dignity of lakhs of cumin farmers of Western Rajasthan and scientific facts." The outcome could set a precedent for how India's GI system distinguishes between places where products are grown and places where they are merely sold.
nri_angle: For diaspora consumers who prize authentic Indian spices, the dispute raises questions about the true origin of cumin and fennel marketed under the Unjha label in international markets.
author: Diaspora Desk
